title: Transfer: Fewest Semesters to Finish Every Course
oneLiner: Take as many courses per semester as you like, once their prerequisites are done. How many semesters? Kahn's algorithm, counted in layers.
keyTakeaway: Run Kahn's algorithm one layer at a time: every task with in-degree 0 right now forms this semester; taking them all lowers their dependents' in-degrees, and the ones that reach 0 form the next semester. The number of layers is the answer, and if some task is never taken there is a cycle, so return -1.
explanation:
This follows Topological Sort: Order Tasks by Dependency with the question changed. There are n courses numbered 0 to n - 1, and each pair [a, b] in prerequisites means a must be finished before b, as in the parent lesson. In one semester you may take any number of courses, as long as all of each one's prerequisites were finished in earlier semesters. Return the fewest semesters needed to take every course, or -1 if it can't be done.

The parent lesson took ready tasks one at a time. Here every ready task should be taken at once, because waiting never helps. So process Kahn's queue in layers: the courses with in-degree 0 at the start are semester 1. Take all of them: for each, decrement the in-degree of every course it unlocks. The courses that reach 0 during this round are exactly the ones whose last prerequisite was just finished, and they form semester 2. Repeat until a round finds nothing new.

In code that is a BFS by levels: note the queue's size at the start of a round, pop exactly that many, and count one semester per round. Keep a count of courses taken. If it ends below n, the rest are stuck on a cycle, the same signal as in the parent lesson, and the answer is -1.

Why is this the fewest? A course can't be taken before the semester after its latest prerequisite, and the layered schedule takes every course at exactly that earliest moment. The number of layers is the number of courses on the longest prerequisite chain. Each course and each edge is handled once: O(V + E) time and space.

The visualization runs n = 7 with prerequisites [5, 0], [0, 1], [6, 1], [1, 2], [3, 2], [2, 4]; the array shows each course's remaining in-degree and the highlighted cells are the current semester.

Explain why the same idea works: before you move on, write two or three sentences comparing this with the parent lesson. What does one layer of Kahn's algorithm mean here, why does taking every ready course at once give the fewest semesters, and why does the same cycle check still work?

Semester 2: take 0. That finishes the last prerequisite of 1, so it is the next semester.
Semester 3: take 1. That finishes the last prerequisite of 2, so it is the next semester.
Semester 4: take 2. That finishes the last prerequisite of 4, so it is the next semester.
Semester 5: take 4. Nothing new becomes ready.
All 7 courses taken in 5 semesters: the longest chain, 5 -> 0 -> 1 -> 2 -> 4, has 5 courses.

recognitionSignals: Tasks with prerequisites that can run in parallel, and the question is how many rounds, stages or time steps are needed.
"Minimum number of semesters", "levels" or "build waves" over a dependency graph.
gotchas: Count rounds, not courses: pop exactly the courses that were ready when the round began.
A course whose in-degree reaches 0 during a round belongs to the next round, not the current one.
If fewer than n courses are ever taken there is a cycle; return -1 rather than the round count.
confusableWith: Topological Sort: Order Tasks by Dependency returns one valid order. This uses the same in-degree bookkeeping but groups the order into layers and counts them.
Multi-Source BFS: Rotting Oranges counts minutes the same way, one BFS level per minute, on a grid instead of a dependency graph.

complexity.note: Kahn's algorithm in layers: every course is queued and taken once and every prerequisite edge decrements one in-degree once. Space is the adjacency list, the in-degree array and the queue.
